GPX photo geotagging on iPhone & iPad

Geotag camera photos with a GPX track—without a computer.

Import a GPX track, choose camera photos already in Apple Photos, and LensPin matches each capture time to the continuous part of the route. Correct the camera clock, inspect every point, and save only the locations you approve.

The 30-second workflow

A route becomes a location timeline.

  1. Import a timestamped GPX fileLensPin parses it locally for valid track points, their UTC timestamps, coordinates, and segment boundaries.
  2. Choose the date range and cameraOnly camera photos without an existing location are candidates. The selected camera make and model must match exactly.
  3. Correct the clock if necessaryApply a fixed offset before date filtering and matching so photos near midnight are not excluded accidentally.
  4. Review the map and evidenceLensPin shows the surrounding route points, time gaps, continuity, suggested point, and any supporting or conflicting iPhone photo.
  5. Save the locations you approveUnselected, unsupported, or already-located photos stay unchanged.

GPX requirements

What the file needs to contain.

1.1

GPX track points

The current parser supports GPX 1.1 track points. A route made only from waypoints or untimed geometry cannot be matched.

UTC

A timestamp for each usable point

Each trkpt needs valid coordinates and a time. GPX timestamps normally represent an absolute UTC instant.

⌁

Continuous, believable segments

Original segment breaks remain hard boundaries. Implausible jumps above 350 m/s create additional safety breaks.

How the suggested point is chosen

Interpolate inside a segment—never across a gap.

Continuous coverage

Between two route points

  • Find the points immediately before and after the capture time
  • Confirm both belong to the same GPX segment
  • Interpolate the coordinate by elapsed time
Gap or edge

Use caution or give no suggestion

  • Do not bridge an original segment break
  • Respect the selected maximum point interval
  • Explain when the photo falls beyond track coverage
A line on a map is not enough.

Two points can look connected visually while their timestamps are hours apart. LensPin uses the time gap and segment structure, not just the drawn geometry.

Clock, time zone, and daylight saving

Why an entire batch can land in the wrong place.

Many cameras store a local wall-clock time without a time-zone offset. A correct-looking time can still refer to the wrong instant after travel or a daylight-saving change.

Camera clock correction

Use the known difference between the camera clock and real time. LensPin applies it only during scanning and matching.

Location time display

Evidence can be displayed in the suggested location's time zone. Automatic lookup may send a small number of coordinates to Apple's geocoding service.

Do not edit the GPX to compensate

Preserve the track's absolute timestamps and correct the camera side of the comparison. This keeps the source evidence auditable.

Test a known photo first

Pick one photo whose place you remember, adjust the offset until it aligns, then review the rest of the batch.

Use both sources together

Let an iPhone photo check the track.

If a geotagged iPhone photo near the same time sits close to the GPX-inferred point, LensPin can treat that agreement as stronger evidence. If the sources are far apart, the suggestion is downgraded and not selected as a safe default.

Within 100 m: supports the trackOver 300 m: conflictNo nearby iPhone photo: GPX stands alone

Current support

What this workflow covers.

iPhone and iPad, iOS 17+

No desktop is required for the LensPin workflow. Long-running background behavior is stronger on iOS 26+.

Static camera photos

Photos/ImageIO-supported JPEG, HEIC, DNG, and RAW assets can be scanned for camera and time metadata. Video is not included in the current version.

Local GPX processing

The GPX file is parsed on the device and is not retained after you restart the workflow.

Suggestions, not recovered truth

The route is evidence for where a photo may belong. Always review unusual gaps, edge matches, and trips with rapid travel.

No track file?

You may still have a useful timeline.

Geotagged iPhone photos taken around the same time can act as location clues.
